item.title: How do we live with each other?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Next week marks one year since The Argument was born. The very first thing we published was an essay of mine called “How do we live with each other?“ It asked the question at the heart of this magazine.

Well-meaning people disagree profoundly on the best way to live. Some of them think you should get married and have children by 22. Others think religion is a poison. Still others believe that eating a hamburger is a grave sin.

These people are often illegible to one another.

So how do we build a society together amid all that disagreement? That is the work of liberalism and is therefore the work of The Argument.

To mark our first anniversary, we’re returning to that founding question with a series about what we owe people whose beliefs and choices we may find difficult to accept or even understand.

Our first piece in this series came out today. In “I don’t need you to believe I’m a woman,” Cassie Pritchard argued that trans rights cannot depend on persuading everyone to share the same beliefs about gender.

Over the next six weeks, we’re going to be publishing writers you know and love — like Kelsey Piper and Matthew Yglesias — as well as some new voices — like Julian Brave Noisecat and Dylan Matthews — all wrestling with this fundamental question.

You’re a free subscriber to The Argument, which means you’ve only seen a fraction of what we have to offer. Over the past year, we’ve built a magazine with original reporting and essays, live events, an innovative polling program, and a flagship piece delivered every weekday.

If you’d like to get everything we have to offer, join us. We’re libbing out.

- Jerusalem

item.title: Does it really matter that we're bowling alone?
item.description: A skeptical debate on social capital
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

“What prepares men for totalitarian domination in the non-totalitarian world is the fact that loneliness, once a borderline experience usually suffered in certain marginal social conditions like old age, has become an everyday experience of the evergrowing masses of our century.”

Hannah Arendt wrote those words in the 1950s, but concern that modern life has become unbearably lonely has reached a fever pitch in recent years. Basically everyone I know and respect (and many I do not) is worried about a crisis of community driven by individual isolation. The generalized concern draws together several otherwise distinct anxieties about modern American life:

  • Kids aren’t partying enough or drinking enough or having enough premarital sex.

  • We spend so much time on our phones and not enough time hanging out with our friends.

  • Nobody knows their neighbors.

  • A decline in social trust seems to be making our politics unbelievably toxic.

I have a knee-jerk aversion to declensionist narratives, so the widespread gloom about an alleged death spiral in American community life makes me suspicious. To begin exploring whether I’m too Pollyannaish about the decline of formal bowling leagues, my co-host Matt Yglesias and I decided to read Bowling Alone (2000) by Robert Putnam.

Putnam’s book argues that American associational life has collapsed dramatically as highly civic older cohorts have died off. There’s very little in the book about bowling leagues per se, but Putnam documents how religious organizations, unions, Rotary clubs, and local organizations of all types have seen their membership fall. Younger cohorts have eschewed the joiner-ism of their parents and grandparents.

The causes of this decline are hotly debated. Putnam largely blames it on generational replacement but also points to TV and suburbanization, among other factors.

Bowling Alone is fixated on the idea of social capital — that associational life is the way that communities build social networks and norms of reciprocity and trustworthiness. As a result, if people aren’t joining bowling leagues anymore, they’re slowly squandering the collective bank of social capital, with dire consequences for all.

I think it’s trivially obvious to point out that people are spending more time alone. Being alone is a lot easier and more fun than it used to be.

But the leap people take from that fact to speculating about mass loneliness and disconnection, the end of democracy and liberalism, and generalized unhealthiness seems half-baked to me. Being alone, feeling lonely, and lacking social capital are related but distinct conditions.

Share

Recent polling from The Argument showed that very few people identify as a lonely person, which directionally supported findings from Pew Research Center that 47% of people say they hardly ever or never feel lonely or isolated. Just 16% say they feel lonely or isolated all or most of the time.

Even if traditional associational social capital has declined, many of the valuable outcomes Putnam attributes to it seem to have survived through other mechanisms. One moving anecdote from early in the book recounts a man donating his kidney to another participant in his bowling league in Ypsilanti, Michigan. Putnam tells this story to illustrate the value of social capital, but that raises the question: Are there fewer people donating kidneys now? No. In 1997, there were 11,701 donations (3,927 from living donors) and in 2025 there were 27,573 (6,521 from living donors).

Other outcomes Putnam points to like crime, dropout rates, teen pregnancies, and premature deaths among children have changed — largely for the better — in the 26 years since he published his book. And it did not take a widespread revival in associational life. At the end of the 544 pages, I was honestly unable to identify a clear reason why I should care about associational life.

Subscribe now

Putnam, like many people worried about social disconnection and the decline of community life, hopes that politics will save us. Throughout the book, he points to increasing political participation as the path forward.

Well, 26 years later and we certainly appear to have a lot more people talking about, thinking about, and working in politics! Has that revived America’s community spirit? You be the judge.

Matt thinks I’m too harsh on Putnam — who correctly understood the threat that watching TV all the time would continue to isolate us — but agrees that some of his prescriptions are wrongheaded.

item.title: The Michigan senate race is Abdul El-Sayed’s to lose
item.description: Our model shows Abdul El-Sayed can survive a "squad"-level underperformance
item.content:encoded:
By Lakshya Jain

The Split Ticket midterms model is updated daily at 5 p.m. Eastern with the latest polls on our website.

We’ve seen a lot of cases where swing-state Republicans nominate ardently ideological, base-aligned candidates over more “establishment” options. Abdul El-Sayed’s primary victory may be the first instance in modern memory where Democrats have done the same in a critical statewide race.

Primary voters are not reflective of the general electorate, and many of those Republicans lost winnable races as a result. But there’s reason to believe El-Sayed’s fate could be different.

There are real risks associated with his candidacy: Our Split Ticket midterms model sees him as a slightly weaker candidate than his primary opponent Rep. Haley Stevens would have been. Stevens had an 80% chance of winning the general election, according to the model, while El-Sayed’s odds are currently at 70%. While we estimate that Stevens would have won by 5.4 percentage points, we think El-Sayed will win by just 3.6 points, thanks to his substantially weaker polling.

Share

Why is El-Sayed still forecast to win, despite his relative weakness? The single biggest reason is a national and state environment that’s uniquely unfriendly to Republicans.

In 2024, when Donald Trump won the popular vote by 1.5 percentage points nationally, Michigan was an R+1 state. Today, that number is closer to D+9 by our estimation (or D+8, if you look at Nate Silver’s modeling). In that sort of environment, even if El-Sayed’s candidate quality is similar to that of the average hardline progressive from “The Squad” (meaning he would perform 5 points worse than a replacement-level Democrat), he would still win.

Are national polls simply wrong about how blue 2026 might be? I don’t think so. Every other indication we’re seeing, ranging from special elections to the Washington state jungle primary, suggests that this really is a blue tsunami of a cycle.1 And in a situation like that, El-Sayed doesn’t need to overperform or even match the baseline performance of generic Democrats. He simply needs to avoid being a disaster.

Can he do that? It’s early, but I’d say the initial signs are promising. He has distanced himself from controversial remarks about 9/11 by Hasan Piker, who campaigned with him. He appears to be embracing party unity and has disavowed his own prior left-wing comments on defunding the police.

In doing so, El-Sayed appears to be avoiding many of the same missteps that plagued Republican firebrands like 2022 Arizona gubernatorial candidate Kari Lake. Also working in El-Sayed’s favor is the fact that Republican nominee Rep. Mike Rogers has made absolutely no effort to distance himself from Trump, flirting with election denial despite running in a state where the president is supremely unpopular.2

That’s why, if you forced me to pick today, I’d say that El-Sayed still wins this race.

Our model is more bullish on El-Sayed than other quantitative forecasts,3 in part because we don’t pay as much attention to pre-primary polling,4 and in part because our generic ballot modeling of Michigan suggests El-Sayed would have to underperform at the level of Elizabeth Warren (who underperformed by 11 points in her last Senate race) in order to lose.

This means he’d have to be nearly twice as weak as the average member of “The Squad,” for whom the typical underperformance is 5 points. While there’s plenty of evidence to suggest El-Sayed is weaker than Stevens would have been, there’s simply no evidence to support the hypothesis he’s that much weaker than a replacement-level Democrat.

This has implications for 2028 as well. Because while election nerds like me will look at overperformance and evaluate whether a win was by “more” or “less” than expected, that’s just not how the median voter looks at things. For a party whose left flank is ascendant, any win from El-Sayed is likely to be held up as proof that their candidates can actually win swing states — and probably gives fuel to the left in the 2028 presidential primaries.

For a long time, candidates like El-Sayed were simply boxed out of Democratic primaries — for anything other than safely blue races — due to concerns about electability as well as struggles with nonwhite segments of the party base. It was this phenomenon that tanked both Warren and Bernie Sanders in the 2020 presidential primary. And if the primary between Stevens and El-Sayed had been held in 2020, it is virtually certain that Stevens — who lost by just 1 percentage point this time — would have won.

But amid the historic unpopularity of both Trump and the Democratic establishment — and in the context of the never-ending conflict in Gaza, which dominated this primary — it is clear that 2026 is a different landscape altogether. Rank-and-file Democrats may well see El-Sayed’s nomination as a relevant test of the left’s ability to win swing states.

Whether that’s true or not, it could have seismic implications for the direction Democrats choose to go in 2028.

item.title: Men also want it all
item.content:encoded:
By Maibritt Henkel

Men are no longer the breadwinners they once were. In 1972, husbands earned more than their wives in at least 85% of American marriages. Husbands were the sole earners in more than half of those.

Today, the share of heterosexual married couples where the man makes more money than the woman has fallen to just 55%. Only 23% of marriages rely solely on a husband’s income. And it’s not just women’s earning potential that has increased their economic independence: Unlike most of their midcentury counterparts, women today can open credit card accounts and take out mortgages without the bank requiring a man’s sign-off.

Some see the rise of the female breadwinner as a bad deal for men. Women may have gained independence, but they have done so at the cost of men’s sense of purpose. “Men are more likely to flourish when they see themselves as providers,” wrote Brad Wilcox, a University of Virginia professor and author of the book Get Married: Why Americans Must Defy the Elites, Forge Strong Families, and Save Civilization, along with co-author Maria Baer. “Men do better when they feel needed — and being a reliable breadwinner makes them feel needed.”

But The Argument’s latest poll of 3,000 registered voters, fielded nationally between July 20 and 26, suggests that an end to male breadwinning might actually suit men’s preferences just fine.

When asked whether they personally agreed or disagreed with the statement “men should be the breadwinner,” just 34% of all male respondents agreed. A substantial majority disagreed.

Share

One explanation for what is going on here is that men are answering out of solidarity with women — or, more cynically, a desire to give the socially desirable response — rather than pure self-interest. They reject the traditional division of labor into male breadwinning and female caregiving because they understand that sharing these responsibilities is good for women.

And yet, when we asked men what was more important to them — career success or getting married and having children — 44% of men prioritized family while 41% prioritized work, around the same shares as women. Among conservative men, the share prioritizing getting married and having children was even higher.

On the right, there is a sense that feminism has forced men into egalitarian relationships they do not want. Traditional marriage gave men a clearly defined role: to provide the primary income to their families. They would like that script back because without it they are in crisis.

Conversely, the left has tended to frame men relinquishing the breadwinner role as a moral imperative. There’s a sense that cheering on their wives’ careers and taking on child care is the least they can do.

Neither framing captures what our polling indicates: that changing gender norms around who spends time at home and who spends time at work might actually align with men’s own interests. Indeed, a majority of fathers say they spend too little time with their children, mostly due to work obligations.

Men don’t know what other men want

The idea that most men want to be breadwinners is not just culturally pervasive — it’s what the men we surveyed think, too. Despite a plurality prioritizing marriage and children themselves, our male respondents overwhelmingly assumed other men prioritized career success.

This is not just a male misperception issue. Women also overestimated the extent to which men prioritize their careers. Seventy-three percent of female respondents said they thought career success was more important to a majority of men than marriage and children, well above what men self-report.

Unsurprisingly, many male respondents also seemed to overestimate how many people agreed with the statement “men should be the breadwinners.” A plurality, 44%, thought the majority of Americans held this belief, while a plurality of female respondents, 46%, felt the opposite. In reality, the share of support among both men and women was much lower, at around 34% and 30%, respectively.

Subscribe now

As in our February poll, there is little evidence in our survey data to suggest that men see traditional gender roles as more favorable than modern egalitarian ones. As Jerusalem Demsas recently pointed out, strong baseline support for gender equality is an underrated fact of our modern political landscape: Around 81% of both male and female respondents agreed that women are equally suited to leadership. Among male respondents who voted for Donald Trump, the share was lower but still 72%.

The family-first MAGA breadwinner

Of course, being a man who values family over career is not the same as being a committed feminist. It is possible to think family is important and also want to reinstitute traditional gender roles. In fact, that seems to be more or less the prescription of today’s conservative thought leaders: Men should care about marriage and family, but they should behave as 1950s breadwinners.

The modern MAGA marriage of “pro-family” policy and masculinist ideals finds some support in our poll. Male Trump voters were considerably more likely to prioritize marriage and children over their careers than male Kamala Harris voters — 57% compared to 33%. They were also much more likely to agree with the statement “men should be the breadwinners,” with 51% endorsing the statement compared to just 15% of their Harris-voting peers.1

In itself, conservative men prioritizing family over career in a survey is not that surprising. What is striking is the gap between these men’s self-reported preference and what they assumed about other men. While over half of male Trump voters said getting married and having children was more important to them than career success, just 24% said this was true of most men.

In other words, conservative men want something for themselves that they think is at odds with what the majority of men want.

There has never been a better time to be a father

The reality is that most people would probably like to have fulfilling family lives as well as meaningful careers.

Having both was very difficult for American women until the late 20th century. Marriage bars — employer policies that barred married women from being hired or retained — were common through the early 1900s. But women’s labor force participation rose from around 40% in the mid-1960s to above 55% just two decades later.

Men also gained something tangible in the family realm over the same period. It is now common — and socially accepted — for fathers to be present during childbirth, push strollers in public, and pick their kids up from school. For children born as late as 1993, 77% of fathers didn’t take a single day of leave after their child was born. For children born between 2014 and 2022, that was true of only 35% of fathers.

The gap in the amount of time American men and women spend with their children has been narrowing for decades. Gen X fathers spent more than twice as much time with their kids as their predecessors did at the same age. Many found this time in part by cutting back daily hours at work.

Prominent voices on the right blame liberalism for rupturing the American family. They argue that its careerist individualism pushed Americans to marry later, have fewer children, and care more about money than anything else. Wilcox has dubbed this the “Midas Mindset,” the idea that “what matters most in your life is building your own individual brand, seeing work as the summit of your life, and steering clear of the encumbrances of family life.”

But to the extent that many men today can embrace being involved parents — who can opt out of the rat race in order to spend more time at home — it is largely thanks to the advances of the women who now contribute much more to household earnings than they used to.

In a world where men do not want to be breadwinners, women joining the labor force is a positive-sum game. If we take men at their word and assume that many of them would quite like to trade time at work for time at home, then discarding traditional gender roles is what makes that possible.

item.title: Who starts a political magazine?
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

Irving Howe, founding editor of Dissent, once quipped that “when intellectuals can do nothing else, they start a magazine.”

The founding of a political magazine is almost inevitably the result of a disaffected spirit. Those with power are too busy running the country and are likely satisfied with existing publications.

But if starting a magazine is a sign of discontent, it is simultaneously an act of hubris. The impulse to write manifestos and screeds, and to make the case for your ideological perspective, may only come to those who can observe the near-infinite amount of content being produced and decide still that they could do better.

The American Prospect openly embraced this impulse in its 1989 prospectus: “The natural reaction to any proposal for a new journal is that we are already swimming in a sea of words: Why more?”

My answer is the same as theirs: Because we are different.

The Prospect wasn’t the first magazine to make this claim,1 and The Argument won’t be the last. On the eve of this magazine’s anniversary, I went back to read the earliest issues of 20th-century political magazines. In the words of a junior writer at National Review: “Flushed with self-importance, we call attention to the fact that this is our First Anniversary issue and confess that we want to talk about it, or better, about ourselves, always an enjoyable way to pass the time.”

Some are more afraid of such overt self-aggrandizement and instead adopt a posture “at once modest and presumptuous,” in the words of Daniel Bell and Irving Kristol in the first issue of The Public Interest (which was something like the Vox of its day).2

Or take this from The New Republic’s opening issue in November 1914: “The New Republic is frankly an experiment.… Its success inevitably depends on public support, but if we are unable to achieve that success under the conditions essential to sound and disinterested thinking, we shall discontinue our experiment and make way for better men.”

That’s nice, but you’ll have to pry this magazine out of my cold, dead hands.

Libs athwart history

Despite founding a liberal publication myself, I recognized The Argument less in the modesty of The New Republic and The Public Interest than in the stridency of their conservative counterparts. It was while reading the latter that I saw my own frustration reflected back to me in biting prose.

Felix Morley, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who left The Washington Post amid growing disagreement over U.S. intervention, co-founded Human Events in 1944. In the opening essay of the conservative anti-interventionist magazine’s first annual bound edition, Morley railed against “journalistic debasement” in coverage of international affairs, going so far as to compare it to Nazi propaganda: “While we have not yet carried these practices as far as did the unlamented Dr. Goebbels, the general direction of governmental propaganda has paid that Nazi leader the sincerest form of flattery.”

Other magazines on the right indulged in similar bluster. The famous one, of course, is National Review’s self-description as “standing athwart history, yelling stop.” Another is Reason magazine, launched in June 1968, which proclaimed: “We accept the responsibility that others have defaulted on. Others preferred to smear the issues with irrelevancies and falsifications. We don’t. Others preferred to be incomprehensible and incoherent. We don’t. Others preferred to ignore your mind. We won’t.”

The resemblance between these upstarts and The Argument is not ideological but positional: Magazines founded to advise a governing status quo can afford modesty, but magazines founded to help build a new paradigm cannot.

Liberalism was ascendant or hegemonic when America’s most significant liberal magazines were founded. The New Republic was started by men who sought to influence President Woodrow Wilson’s administration; The Public Interest was founded right after President Lyndon B. Johnson’s landslide victory and the triumph of civil rights legislation. While The American Prospect began publication in 1990 after three consecutive Republican presidential victories, small-l liberalism was still dominant: Democrats controlled Congress, the Cold War was coming to an end, and liberal democracy was on the rise around the world.

National Review, on the other hand, was founded as conservatism sought to claw its way back to relevance. The New Deal settlement had entrenched itself so thoroughly that, under the banner of what he called Modern Republicanism, President Dwight D. Eisenhower expanded Social Security, raised the federal minimum wage, and broadened unemployment-insurance coverage from within the GOP.

Reviewing these decades-old essays has also reminded me how far magazines can stray from their original purpose. Reason, once an Objectivist magazine, is now best characterized as libertarian; Commentary, once the flagship of liberal anti-Stalinism, is now a hawkish neoconservative outfit.

Part of what made The Argument necessary is that I found little of liberalism left in outlets like The American Prospect. In its 1989 prospectus, the latter called markets invaluable and defended the moniker “liberal” against attempts to rebrand as “progressive” or “populist”: “Denying the ‘liberal label’ suggests embarrassment and shame more than open-mindedness.” Now, the Prospect’s “about” page says it is devoted to the “progressive perspective.” Long gone is the magazine’s healthy respect for the market mechanism.3 Its editorial leadership is in the thrall to neo-Brandeisian economic populism and wouldn’t even take a clean stand against President Donald Trump’s illegal (and unpopular) tariffs.

It is a dark time for liberalism. The Trump administration has dispatched federal agents against law-abiding American citizens, lied brazenly to the courts, and begun dismantling the twin engines of progress: immigration and scientific research. Elite resistance to this assault on the American system is divided among left-wing populists with a tenuous relationship to basic tenets of liberty, centrist Democrats who lack any positive vision, and a dying breed of right-liberals.

Long liberalism

The Argument’s task is not to debate the policy agenda of an establishment that shares our commitments, but to make the case for a completely different paradigm. Things may seem dire, but I’m long liberalism:

  • No other ideology has been capable of delivering mass prosperity, economic growth, and scientific progress while protecting and expanding civil rights.

  • Despite decades of elite hostility to markets, capped off by Trump’s tariff regime, Americans remain committed to key tenets of economic liberalism and its promise of abundance.

  • In defiance of efforts to divide us by race, religion, and origin, Americans continue to believe that rights belong to individuals, that the law should treat us as equals, and that anyone can become fully and equally American.

While there are many individual liberals scattered throughout the great magazines and newspapers of this country, none of those publications offers a clear institutional voice willing to engage in the type of ideological combat necessary to rebuild American liberalism.

One thing I share with all the great political magazine founders, from the socialist dissenters to the Ayn Rand obsessives, is a belief in the power of ideas.

Howe, the Dissent editor whose line about intellectuals starting a magazine is oft-quoted, had more to say. In the very next sentence, he adds: “But starting a magazine is also doing something: at the very least it is thinking in common. And thinking in common can have unforeseen results.”4

The Argument is a bet on readers like you: ones who believe in a vision of liberalism abandoned by the current factions in American politics, who treasure rigorous, public debate as a tool for advancing the best ideas, and who are excited to be a part of a community as varied as this one. In the years to come, we’re going to keep picking fights and running polls and publishing pathbreaking essays. Thanks for libbing out with us.

In recent decades, we’ve faced many crises of social connection: the loneliness epidemic, the deaths-of-despair phenomenon, the effects of phones on teens. But before all these, the source text for civic atrophy was Robert Putnam’s Bowling Alone, which documented a decline in U.S. associational life. No more bowling leagues, no more Rotary Clubs. Our chief malady, Putnam argued, was a decline in “social capital.”

Jerusalem is skeptical. This week on the pod, Jerusalem and Matt reassess one of the foundational texts of the 21st century and argue about how relevant it is to our current afflictions. Click below to see how it holds up:

Lakshya Jain hosted Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet from Michigan’s 8th District. In their discussion, she shared some tricks of the trade. First, she emphasized how different primary and general electorates are. But the tip that hooked me was this one: She has a burner phone so she can escape the algorithm and listen to people outside of her ideological lane.

What’s News with The Argument

The Argument recommends, by Kobe Yank-Jacobs

Politicians never change their minds. They “evolve” on the issues. But here at The Argument, sometimes — just sometimes — we do change our minds. In fact, we even grow as people. New things appeal to us, old passions fade out.

That’s what I wanted to capture in this week’s recommendations section.

I asked the team to share media with social commentary that they used to agree with, and immediately, our social media director, Megha Fernandes, nailed it on my highly specific request:

This is a painting known as The Singing Butler by Jack Vettriano. So, um, what’s the social commentary here? you might ask. At first, Megha saw none either.

“To me, it was a beautiful depiction of being so in love that nothing else mattered,” she said. “The couple at the center didn’t even seem to notice the rain since they were too caught up in dancing together.”

But when she returned to her parents’ house as an adult, where a print hangs on the wall, she saw it differently. This was “class warfare,” she asserted over drinks at a team hangout the other night.

“Were they paid fairly? Did they even want to be out there?” she asked of the butler and the maid. “Suddenly, it seemed a lot easier for the couple to dance carefree in the rain when someone else was standing by, waiting with an umbrella.”

What I loved about Megha’s take was how closely she was reading the image. It prompted other teammates to take a second look at works they used to find meaning in.

It brought Jerusalem Demsas back to her own teenage radicalism. The social commentary she renounced? “Baby, I’m an Anarchist” by Against Me. For the record, she still thinks it’s a great song but declines to endorse the message.

“I no longer stand behind teenage Jerusalem's disdain for people who wouldn't throw rocks through Starbucks windows or hurl Molotov cocktails.”

God bless the parents of all teenagers.

Milan Singh followed this with an influential teenage experience of his own. He read The Omnivore’s Dilemma by Michael Pollan and became a vegetarian for five years. In his case, he doesn’t renounce the decision. In fact, he wishes he could stick with it. It’s just that, when he got to college, he found it hard to put on muscle on his ethical diet.

For my part? I actually had a few items in consideration, but the question to the team was motivated by a joyous car ride I spent relistening to Father John Misty’s 2017 album Pure Comedy. This is perhaps among the most wry and timely albums of social commentary I can imagine. It skewers the social media age in songs like “Total Entertainment Forever,” which closes:

When the historians find us we’ll be in our homes /
plugged into our hubs /
skin and bones, /
a frozen smile on every face /
as the stories replay /
This must have been a wonderful place

At the time, I was a self-branded Luddite, refusing as many conveniences of phones as I could manage while maintaining a college social life. Almost a decade later, it’s not so much that I disagree as that I’m resigned. I look back on my fickle resistance and finally understand Misty’s tone.

It’s ironic, in part, because in every song, his knowing speaker also participates in the shallow society he dismisses. He has to. How else can you be a good critic? So far away from the thing you critique?

As the team concluded our chat, weaving in and out of old anecdotes, I started to appreciate how much people treasured the items they’d stepped away from. It reminded me of a line from a Simon & Garfunkel song.5 “After changes upon changes we are more or less the same. / After changes, we are more or less the same.”

We have quarter-zips, keychains, hats, and stickers. Each one is a great conversation starter in its own way. Buy them here.

1

Commonweal, a liberal Catholic magazine founded in 1924, opened its first issue by sheepishly noting: “The question will naturally arise why the editors of The Commonweal believe there is room for another journal to discuss public affairs, to review the important publications of the day, and produce original fiction, essays and poetry. … We believe that The Commonweal will be so fundamentally different to our contemporaries that in place of competition in an over-crowded field we shall occupy a position that hitherto has been left vacant.” With all the love in the world, many such cases!

2

Bell and Kristol admit they’re probably going to write some boring stuff: “...just as not all mathematical problems are exciting (intellectually, aesthetically, emotionally), so not all social problems are, either. Only the incurably adolescent mind will find this fact of life distressing. Unfortunately, there are always more adolescent minds than adolescents around.”

3

See the Prospect‘s prospectus, which directly calls market mechanisms “invaluable,” treats markets and democratic politics as complementary, and acknowledges that liberals in another context might favor “greater reliance on market forces.”

See also Arthur Schlesinger Jr.’s opening salvo for the Prospect: “The liberal answers of the past were not infallible. Affirmative government sometimes tried to do too much. Regulations became intrusive and burdensome. Government programs miscarried. And the public interest, liberals must understand, is something more than, and very often different from, the sum of the interests of organized groups in our society.”

See also Cass Sunstein’s 1990 piece calling the private market “usually an engine of individual freedom and economic welfare.”

4

Commentary likened editors to “well-diggers”: “We roll up our sleeves and in the sweat of our brows, we dig. And if the time and place are right, and the omens are propitious — of a sudden, fresh, cool, flowing waters.… To this task, soberly and earnestly, we dedicate ourselves.”

5

This line is only available in certain live versions of the song, “The Boxer.” It was replaced by a horn solo in the recording.

item.title: No, Senator Murphy, I don't want to join your cult.
item.description: Politics isn't where you should find meaning.
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Editor’s note: The first essay The Argument ever published asked, “How do we live with each other?” To mark our first anniversary on Aug. 17, we’re returning to that founding question with a series about what we owe people whose beliefs and choices we may find difficult to accept or even understand. Over the next six weeks, familiar voices at The Argument and new voices alike will approach that question from different angles.

Today’s essay is mine. Taking U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy’s recent book as a starting point, I examine the growing obsession with the common good among the postliberal right and left.

To receive every essay in this series, subscribe today.

– Jerusalem Demsas

U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy’s new book Crisis of the Common Good: The Fight for Meaning and Connection in a Broken America subverts the norms of its genre. Politicians who seemingly aspire to higher office tend to focus on sharing their biography and bland, poll-tested policy prescriptions.

Murphy, to his credit, did not bore me.

In the prose of an AI that has been trained on religious texts but is itself not an embodied soul, Murphy calls for a “cult of the common good” that we can worship instead of “false idols” like technology or profit. In his chapter outlining what his “cult of the common good” would look like, Murphy favorably recounts the following anecdote from Puritan Massachusetts:

“In 1639, a local shopkeeper named Robert Keayne became the subject of great public shame for charging eight pence for six-penny nails. According to Winthrop, ‘the cry of the country was so great’ against this attempted price gouging that Keayne faced trial before the General Court, which fined him £200 (an exorbitant sum), and then an ecclesiastical trial before his own church, which publicly admonished him for ‘selling his wares at excessive rates, to the dishonor of God’s name.’ He narrowly escaped excommunication—a sentence the colony imposed on eight people for economic offenses during this period.”

Murphy presents this anecdote as an indictment of modern-day America, where we have a constitutional prohibition against excessive fines and maintain separation between church and state. I was curious, though, about those other people charged with economic offenses and discovered the story of Ann Hibbens.

The trouble for Hibbens began when she “questioned the bill from her carpenter.” Despite winning a civil lawsuit, Hibbens was censured by her church for her “abrasive” behavior in court.

Historian Monica D. Fitzgerald recounts Hibbens’ tale, arguing that Hibbens was doomed in part because of her gender, citing one church leader who complained, “More offensive than any of her sins, she has one sin worthy of reproof: and that is transgressing the rule of the Apostle in usurping authority over him whom God hath made her head and husband and in taking the power and authority which God hath given to him out of his hands.”

She was eventually excommunicated. Years later, after her husband died, she was tried as a witch and hanged.

Now, obviously, I don’t think Murphy supports hanging women for witchcraft. Nor does punishing someone for price gouging necessarily lead to witch trials. But it’s also not an accident that a community with enough coercive power to punish someone for charging a lot for nails ends up using that coercive power in other realms of life as well. The regulation of prices, religious orthodoxy, and women’s behavior all stemmed from the same view: that “the community” could define the good, interpret dissent as moral disorder, and punish the dissenter.

Murphy repeatedly calls for a “cult of the common good,” only to retreat from his own language by assuring the reader that he is “half-joking.” Each chapter is organized around a cult Murphy is criticizing. As a writer, I sympathize with becoming overly committed to parallelism, and perhaps that’s what happened here.

But the metaphor is more revealing than he intends. A community may influence its members, impose obligations, and cultivate shared values. But a cult claims something more comprehensive: authority to tell its members what is true, what their lives are for, and how they must live them.

I could not find a clear explanation of what would limit the jurisdiction of Murphy’s cult. A liberal order begins with the presumption of freedom — yes, including economic freedom — and then requires public justification when the government chooses to intervene (often for good reason!).

The cult of the common good reverses that presumption. It begins with an Official Version of the Good Life and then treats the law and politics as the way to direct people toward it.

Subscribe now

Who gets to decide the common good?

What’s odd is that Murphy seems to understand the danger of political leaders defining the good life when it’s someone else’s definition.

At one point in his book, the senator recalls “wincing” when he heard then-President Barack Obama try to nudge people onto his version of the good life: “Tonight, I ask every American to commit to at least one year or more of higher education or career training.” Murphy says that this challenge didn’t recognize the plurality of paths to achievement: “others seek different routes into the job market.” Murphy argues that this “helped cement a stigma against those who could not achieve a higher degree.”

Yet, in the very same book, Murphy calls for requiring six months of national service for every young American.

All Obama did was make an appeal, and Murphy condemns it for stigmatizing people who are on other paths. Yet, Murphy’s plan is not only to stigmatize paths he disagrees with but also to ban them and create one government-approved option for young people.

An American who ignored Obama’s challenge faced no material consequences. What happens to one who refuses Murphy’s? He doesn’t say.

Murphy’s objection, then, is not really to political leaders defining the good life; it is to someone else defining it differently. Many such cases.

American Compass founder Oren Cass, whom Murphy cites favorably in his book, is similarly excited to reorient society around the common good. He’s useful to consider because he provides more detailed examples of what it looks like to reassemble politics and policy around a cult of the common good.

Cass’ work reveals that, in his view, common-good politics entails using culture and government to privilege particular ways of living and to orient individual behavior toward those predetermined paths.

Earlier this year, American Compass released a manifesto arguing that to revive American citizenship we need to “[offer] individuals well-defined paths down which they can confidently and successfully travel.”

I publicly pressed Cass to explain what those well-defined paths were and how governments should restrain people who rejected them. The most banal reading could just claim this as the status quo — we do not let people go around murdering others willy-nilly.

But clearly Cass means something more than that. While every policy decision contains within it implicit nudges, there is a world of difference between a government oriented around making it easier for people to live the lives they choose and a government that preordains certain paths and punishes you if you fall out of line.

The Cost-of-Thriving Index is a tool created by Cass and American Compass as a “better way to understand the challenge for working families” than typical inflation-based adjustments. One important choice Cass makes is to build the index around a male earner’s paycheck.

His reasoning is that it holds “constant the economic experience of a group that traditionally has been recognized as the family breadwinner” whereas an aggregate wage “experiences downward pressure from a ‘mix shift’ as women account for more of the workforce.”1

But Cass’ index embeds a particular ideal of middle-class life: a family supported by one male breadwinner. On the index’s own 2022 figures, a couple earning the median male and female wages would make about $115,000 — enough to cover their $76,000 basket with nearly $40,000 left before taxes. Cass’ index treats a two-income household as evidence of failure.

And if you think the common good is constrained by the law, think again. On “Liberation Day,” when Trump unilaterally enacted his illegal tariffs, Cass celebrated, writing that they “lay the groundwork for a new set of arrangements … that prioritize the national interest and the flourishing of the nation’s working families.”

Subscribe now

Good-faith people disagree with each other

Despite my deep disagreements with them, I think both Cass and Murphy are good people trying to figure out the best way to improve the country. So how do we end up in such different places?

In part, this is because of empirical disagreements that we might be able to hash out if we were so inclined. But a large part of our disagreement comes from the fact that different people, reasoning well, often end up believing very different things. Edmund Fawcett identified that part of the liberal tradition as the “acknowledgment of inescapable ethical and material conflict within society.”

There is no final debate round where you will convince everyone that your economic project is right. There is no homogeneous community that will one day arise, content to live under the same economic, political, and social paradigm. Even within the same families, siblings raised together will come away with very different ideas about how best to conduct themselves.

As political philosopher Charles Larmore put it, “reasoning about ethical matters, once it goes beyond platitudes and seeks some precision, is as likely to drive us apart as to bring us together.”

Once you accept this fact about the world, the question of political philosophy reveals itself to be: What are legitimate exercises of power?

Where should we find meaning?

I am a Christian. I believe in God, I go to church, I pray, and I volunteer with my congregation. When I’m facing a difficult decision, I usually call my father, who will help guide me through it using our shared moral principles and framework. This is where I find meaning.

Religion serves (at least) three functions:

  1. Epistemological: God is an authority through which we can understand what is true.

  2. Ontological: God tells us what is real and meaningful. Why are we on this planet? What is our purpose?

  3. Ethical: God tells us how to live. What is good and evil? What duties do we have to our neighbors?

You do not have to be religious to have those functions fulfilled. There are people who have very strong ethical codes by which they live and friends and family who share that moral code with them.

One modern secular example is the effective altruist community. It has a well-developed moral philosophy (complete with priests!), it has a faith community within which its adherents actively debate their theology (complete with sects!), and it has clear ways of applying its theology to people’s everyday lives to help them act rightly.

Meaning is important, and if you lack it in your life, I do not think it will be easy to live happily or well, however you define those concepts. But where I depart from Murphy’s call for meaning-making is that politics isn’t where people should find meaning.

“If America is going to worship any idol, let it be the common good,” writes Murphy.

I’m not even totally sure what this means, but I can heartily say: No. This would be bad.

Recent presidential elections have divided the electorate closely. Nearly half of the electorate is disappointed when the winner is announced. In what world, then, does victory constitute a mandate to define a small set of paths? As the parties have sorted more consistently along ideological lines, elections have taken on greater stakes.

Many of my favorite political leaders have been overt about their own morality. In his second inaugural address, Abraham Lincoln urged “firmness in the right as God gives us to see the right,” while calling for “malice toward none” and “charity for all.”

I want political leaders whose moral convictions constrain their exercise of power, not leaders who use power to impose their moral convictions.

A senator can make it easier to raise a child, but he cannot tell us why we should have one. He can protect our freedom to worship, but he cannot give us religion. He can regulate hospitals, but he can’t tell us when to move our ailing parents into hospice.

Politics shouldn’t create meaning, it should make room for it.

More in the How do we live with each other? series:

1

Of course, if Cass were genuine about wanting to filter out composition effects, as economist Matt Darling pointed out, you would build this measure solely around women’s wages.

item.title: Rich and poor kids should grow up next to each other
item.content:encoded:
By Milan Singh

Editor’s note: The first essay The Argument ever published asked, “How do we live with each other?” To mark our first anniversary on Aug. 17, we’re returning to that founding question with a series about what we owe people whose beliefs and choices we may find difficult to accept or even understand. Over the next six weeks, familiar voices at The Argument and new voices alike will approach that question from different angles.

Today, Milan Singh takes this question literally by exploring the way that affordable housing policy in the United States incentivizes economic segregation. How should we live with each other? Right next to each other, Singh argues.

To receive every essay in this series, subscribe today.

– Jerusalem Demsas

Poor kids in America tend to grow up in a totally different world from middle-class and rich kids. They often grow up in higher-crime neighborhoods, with friends whose parents are unemployed, and attending substandard schools.

Growing up in this separate world can make poverty harder to escape. A growing body of research suggests that where children live — and who they grow up around — can profoundly shape their prospects as adults.

That has massive implications for American affordable housing policy. Most affordable housing in America is old housing. New affordable housing is almost entirely built with the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit (LIHTC) and concentrates poverty in 100% affordable housing projects in high-poverty neighborhoods.

Projects with 100% affordable housing can sound good to some people. But in practice, they mean segregating low-income families away from the very neighborhoods that would give their children equality of opportunity.

Share

To others, the idea of allowing low-income families to move into their neighborhood sounds like a threat. Don’t poor people bring crime? Won’t they undermine good public schools? Community cohesion?

I want to make the case for living right next to each other by building class-integrated communities. Currently, U.S. housing policy isn’t well designed to optimize for this goal. But the benefits of integration — for the rich in addition to the poor — are likely large enough that we should refocus housing policy toward promoting the development of mixed-income neighborhoods.

Location, location, location

When it comes to low-income housing, location is not just another amenity like in-unit laundry or plentiful natural light. That’s because research suggests that whether poor families can achieve upward mobility largely depends on where they live.

From 1994 to 1998, the Department of Housing and Urban Development ran an experiment called “Moving to Opportunity” (MTO), where families living in high-poverty neighborhoods were given vouchers to move into very low-poverty neighborhoods. MTO provided ideal conditions to study the effects of place-based low-income housing policy both because of the large number of participants (over 4,600 families) and because detailed tax data on these families allowed researchers to track children’s adult outcomes.

In a 2016 paper, economists Raj Chetty, Nathaniel Hendren, and Lawrence F. Katz studied the adult economic outcomes of poor children who moved as part of the program compared with those who didn’t. Children who moved into low-poverty neighborhoods before turning 13 went on to earn 34% more on average than children who were left behind. The former were also more likely to attend college (and to attend better colleges compared with the college-bound in the control group), more likely to live in high-income neighborhoods as adults, and less likely to become single parents.

In fact, the lifetime earnings increases for children in the MTO group were so large that the program paid for itself: The increase in tax revenues was greater than the initial voucher costs.

Follow-up research established that these beneficial effects were mainly driven by the children’s exposure to their new neighborhoods.

If a child from a poor neighborhood moved to a high-income neighborhood at birth, that would wipe out 80% of the expected earnings gap between them and the children born in the rich neighborhood. The benefits of moving to greener pastures scale with the amount of time spent in the new neighborhood.

Subscribe now

But what exactly is going on here? What about these neighborhoods is changing the fortunes of these children so dramatically? It might be integration, but it could also just be better schools or low crime rates. If it’s the latter, then the solution might be educational reforms or better policing. We could just try to improve poor neighborhoods, in other words, without worrying about socioeconomic integration.

But in follow-up research published in 2022, Chetty and a different team of co-authors found that what really matters is something a lot harder to envision without thorough integration: cross-class friendships.

Using anonymized data from 21 billion Facebook friendships, Chetty and his team were able to measure the degree of cross-class friendships in locations across the country — basically, the share of a poor person’s friends who are rich.

They tested a bunch of things to see what was driving these positive benefits. Traditional measures of social capital like volunteering, the presence of civic organizations, and even the presence of tightly knit friendship networks mattered little for predicting whether poor kids would do better as adults. What mattered most was the prevalence of cross-class friendships.

The mechanism by which cross-class friendships generate greater upward mobility seems to be through exposure to adult role models. In a 2025 paper, Chetty found that the strongest predictor of children’s adult economic outcomes was the employment rates of the parents of other children their age in their neighborhoods — parents of the cohort they are most likely to make friends with. In places with increasing parental employment rates, adult outcomes for children improved; in places where parental employment was falling, children did worse as adults.

Integration is probably positive-sum

I grew up in Cambridge, Massachusetts. My high school is in the 87th percentile for cross-class friendships, using Chetty’s metric. Cambridge is an increasingly expensive place to live, but that’s largely a result of its economic success running up against the relatively inelastic supply of housing.1

Growing up, all of my friends’ parents were employed (in a variety of occupations), and none of them used drugs or went to prison. The public school system was pretty good, and there were lots of adults around who had gone to Harvard, Yale, or MIT. This made me think that, since I was generally good at school, I could do this too, provided I applied myself.

Though I may not have actually needed this network — after all, my parents went to good colleges too — I still benefited.

I also grew up with friends who lived in public housing, whose parents had blue-collar jobs, or who chose to join the military instead of going to college after high school. I went to a fancy college where most of my classmates were from families like mine, but I’m very grateful that some of my closest friends are from families who aren’t — who have ambitions and dreams that are very different from my own. My perspective on life is all the richer for having grown up with them.

I share my own experience in part because it’s hard to imagine the socioeconomic integration of high-opportunity neighborhoods without the buy-in of the comfortable families who already live there — people who worry that an influx of poor families might change the character of their neighborhoods in ways they don’t want.

Concerns about the economic, fiscal, and criminal impacts of newcomers aren’t always the pure result of racism or classism. For example, an influx of new students into local public schools — students who may be below grade level in certain subjects — may strain teachers and reduce the amount of attention given to longtime residents’ children.

Subscribe now

A 1976 U.S. Commission on Civil Rights report contains contemporaneous interviews with students, parents, and administrators going through integration. White students reported fear and anxiety about entering a different school with protesting adults causing chaos. They also complained of long and inconvenient transportation.

One Tampa student had to wake up at 4:45 a.m. to take the assigned bus. But, overall, reading through the report reveals that students were frustrated by media reports exaggerating the racial overtones of ordinary conflict and reported positive experiences with integration. One white Stamford student even called integration “the best thing that ever happened to me.”

But the research we have on both school and residential integration suggests that such concerns are probably overblown.

During Jim Crow, Black children were far worse off than white children on average: Their families were poorer, their life expectancies were lower, and their neighborhoods had much higher violent crime rates. There were widespread fears that the socioeconomic integration implied by racial desegregation would have negative effects on white students if their schools became more exposed to the problems of poverty.

Instead, research showed that court-ordered school desegregation “significantly increased both educational and occupational attainments, college quality and adult earnings, reduced the probability of incarceration, and improved adult health status” for Black people whose schools were integrated — while having “no effects on whites” who attended the same schools.

Of course, “no effects” just refers to the sorts of things economists can measure, like standardized test scores or earnings or health outcomes. Subjective experiences matter too. A 2004 qualitative study based on interviews with 242 graduates of desegregated high schools, including 136 white graduates, is useful here.

The white graduates described greater appreciation for other cultures, greater comfort and social competence in diverse settings, less fear of people of color, and less reliance on racial stereotypes. It’s good to take this with a grain of salt — few people in 2004 were going to admit to having hated integration — but this tracks with my experience as well: It’s nice to grow up and live with people who are different from you.

According to a different 2004 paper in the American Economic Review, there is “no evidence of an impact of [busing Black students to formerly white schools] on white students in receiving districts.” In particular, test scores for incumbent white students showed no decline.

Of course, the applicability of race-based school integration to class-based residential integration may be limited. But a recent paper from Chetty’s research lab, Opportunity Insights, provides further evidence that the positive effects of integration do not come at the advantaged group’s expense.

The paper analyzed HOPE VI — a federal program intended to turn distressed public housing projects into mixed-income communities — and found that, when wealthier people move into the revitalized public housing projects, the low-income neighborhoods hosting the projects become more socially integrated, and resident children earn more as adults.

And within wealthy neighborhoods, there’s no correlation between greater class integration and how much rich children earn as adults. In other words, the evidence suggests that integration is probably positive-sum overall.

To be clear, these findings are not dispositive evidence against every potential downside of neighborhood integration. I don’t think we can eliminate the possibility that, past a certain level, integration has costs for rich children. What we do know is that gradual efforts at integration — the kind tested in the MTO experiment — are unlikely to impose substantial costs on rich kids and will provide very large benefits for poor children.

Beyond public vs. private

There are two ways the government could promote economic integration: It could build and operate mixed-income housing itself, or it could provide vouchers to poor families so they can afford a place in a nicer neighborhood. Because vouchers are a more efficient use of public funds, and because of the benefits of economic integration, we should prefer the latter option.

But vouchers alone aren’t enough to achieve economic integration. After all, poor families might not be aware of which neighborhoods provide the greatest boost to economic mobility, or they may not have the time to tour apartments in faraway neighborhoods and fill out applications. Landlords may be unwilling to rent to voucher-holders.

Subscribe now

In a 2018 to 2019 experiment, Chetty’s team at Opportunity Insights partnered with public housing authorities in Seattle and King County, Washington. In the first phase, one group of housing voucher recipients was provided with information about high-opportunity neighborhoods, financial assistance, customized support services during the moving process, and connections with landlords; the other group was just provided with housing vouchers. Among the group receiving the full support services, the share that moved to high-opportunity neighborhoods was 53%, compared with 15% in the control group.

The intervention in the experiment is estimated to have increased lifetime earnings by an average of $212,000. After accounting for increased tax revenue and higher voucher spending caused by families moving to areas with higher rents, the researchers found that each dollar of government spending on the program increased the incomes of voucher recipients by $1.35.

That sounds pretty good to me, but there is a third option for achieving integration: the government could simply dictate where people live. Singapore has been able to do it, but only by having 80% of the population live in public housing subject to strict quotas to force ethnic integration. That is, to put it mildly, unlikely to fly in the United States.

This is a free country, and people should have the freedom to live where they want to. But, to the extent that the government is in the business of subsidizing housing for the poor — and I think it should be — policy should encourage greater integration.

We are very far from that at the moment. The Low-Income Housing Tax Credit — the main way we build new affordable housing in this country — financed just under 4 million affordable housing units between 1986 and 2024. And it incentivizes building 100% low-income housing in neighborhoods that are already poor.

Without going too deep into the weeds, the basic reason why this happens is that developers must pay substantial fixed costs to participate in the LIHTC program; these costs include hiring attorneys to ensure that projects meet state-set standards when applying for the credits, arranging financing, and verifying the incomes of tenants. Crucially, these costs are essentially fixed regardless of the share of units in a project that are affordable (meaning leased at below-market rates), while the tax credits can only be applied toward the costs of building the affordable units.

This makes it unrealistic to build mixed-income projects with LIHTC money, since the developer would be paying the full costs of compliance while only receiving a partial subsidy.2 There are also incentives to locate projects in high-poverty neighborhoods.

The structure of LIHTC does more than discourage mixed-income housing. It uses public money to reinforce the economic segregation that housing policy should be trying to overcome.

We do not need to dictate where people live. But we should stop making segregation the default. Affordable housing policy should give poor families a real chance to live in high-opportunity neighborhoods — and give poor, middle-class, and rich kids a chance to grow up in the same world.

Subscribe now

Recommended reading:

1

This is because of zoning.

2

There are two other factors worth discussing briefly. First, because arranging LIHTC deals is incredibly complicated — take a look at Figure 1 on page 5 of this Urban Institute report — a highly specialized industry of financial institutions, law firms, and affordable housing developers has sprung up. These firms are specialized in building 100% affordable projects, so they may lack the specialized knowledge required to build mixed-income projects. Second, it is not clear whether there is that much market demand for mixed-income buildings. It is plausible that many rich people don’t want to live in a building with a high share of affordable units. This isn’t necessarily a problem; based on the Chetty research, what matters for upward mobility is integration at the neighborhood, not at the building level.

item.title: No one is buying the right-wing theory of the elite
item.description: What Bernie Sanders gets right about billionaires
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

After 75 years of conservative attacks on college professors, journalists, and bureaucrats, hardly anyone — including Trump voters — calls those groups elite.

Way back in 1951, conservative William F. Buckley Jr. wrote God and Man at Yale, a book that tarred his alma mater as a hotbed of left-wing radicalism: “The institution that derives its moral and financial support from Christian individualists … persuad[es] the sons of these supporters to be atheistic socialists.”

Spiro Agnew, President Richard Nixon’s vice president, called network news leaders a “small and unelected elite” for being hostile to the president’s message. Irving Kristol, the father of neoconservatism, defined an elite “new class” including teachers, journalists, social workers, foundation staff, and bureaucrats.

Today, the standard-bearer of the left-wing-elite theory is surely the Manhattan Institute’s Christopher Rufo, who has turned his ire on “a small number of people with influence in the knowledge-based institutions” who are acting “in their own interest and against the interest of the vast majority of the American people.”

Share

Rufo has compared his project to Nixon’s to “tame the national bureaucracy” and dismantle “radical organizations.”

But despite decades of effort on this front, according to The Argument‘s most recent poll, elite basically means billionaire or celebrity to the majority of American voters — including Trump 2024 voters:

It’s clear from this data that the Buckley-Nixon-Rufo project has had some effect on Republican voters: Trump 2024 voters are 11 percentage points more likely to view journalists as part of the elite than Harris 2024 voters, 5 points more likely to view government employees as part of the elite, and 13 points more likely to view college professors as part of the elite.

Still, none of these categories crack 20% for Trump voters.

When I was designing this poll with our director of political data, Lakshya Jain, I was particularly interested in going deeper. Not just “Who are the elite?” but “What are the public’s perceptions of elites?”

We discovered a strong correlation between elites and “people who hold positions I don’t like.” “Elite” is not just a socioeconomic category; it carries negative baggage.

Subscribe now

Trump voters overwhelmingly imagined elites to be more liberal than the country, while Harris voters overwhelmingly imagined them to be more conservative. Forty-nine percent of Trump voters placed elites to the country’s left, compared with just 21% who placed them to its right. Among Harris voters, the pattern reversed: 68% said elites were more conservative, while only 10% said they were more liberal.

As a result, the “elite worldview” produced by our poll results was ideologically incoherent, a grab bag of positions from both sides.

Sixty-six percent of voters support government-provided health insurance for all Americans, yet 59% think elites oppose it.

Eighty-one percent of voters think men and women are equally suited to leadership, yet 50% of voters think elites disagree with that statement.

Just 11% of voters support government ownership of most businesses, but 28% attribute that position to elites.

The public’s picture of elite opinion, then, looks like a map of beliefs that ordinary voters find objectionable.

While this is ideologically incoherent, it is consistent. Elites believe what ordinary people reject; therefore, since ordinary people are ideologically incoherent, so too are elites.

I also don’t want to overstate the incoherence here — voters are remarkably consistent — across party, class, race, age, and every other demographic we polled — about the category of person that qualifies as elite: billionaires and celebrities yes, but to a lesser extent politicians and businessmen.

Subscribe now

The strangest part of all this: In such an environment, how does a billionaire, celebrity, politician, businessman — the poster child for what is considered elite — become president not once, but twice?

Notably, Trump is incredibly unpopular, so I wouldn’t call what he’s doing a strategy for success. But it does call into question how much our poll is really capturing about anti-elite politics.

Many people viewed 2016 as an election where the public overthrew the liberal elite — personified in Yale alumna and former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton. Trump himself explicitly presented the election as ordinary Americans reclaiming power from a corrupt establishment.

There are many ways to interpret these findings all together, but my interpretation is that hostility to elites only explains a small part of electoral outcomes. Particularly in 2016, the sense was that Trump was aligned with many of the relevant swing voters on certain issues like immigration and trade.1

After we dropped this poll, my co-host Matt Yglesias was excited to talk about it on the podcast. During our conversation, he argued that elite status should be defined by consequential decision-making power. We also debated the most interesting part of the poll (to me): what the celebrity findings mean for political and cultural change.

item.title: JD Vance's economic pitch is higher prices
item.description: The vice president's heterodox idea to pay more for a Honda
item.content:encoded:
By Jerusalem Demsas

Welcome to The Closing Argument, our verdict on the news, plus everything The Argument published and appeared in this week.

The Verdict, by Jerusalem Demsas

There’s an entire Wikipedia article devoted to the term “Exorbitant privilege.” It’s not about the advantages tall people enjoy at concerts or that models have in the dating market.

No, it refers to the fact that everybody wants the U.S. dollar.

People, governments, and banks like to hold U.S. currency because people trust that it will continue to hold value. That trust comes from our geopolitical dominance, the size of our economy, our deep financial markets, and, uh, political stability.

This exorbitant privilege is the subject of many long academic articles. But to keep it short: It makes it cheaper to borrow, makes it easier for us to enforce sanctions, and makes it cheaper to buy foreign goods.1

Share

Vice President JD Vance, crusader against structural advantage that he is, is not impressed with the benefits that flow to Americans from this arrangement. In a 2023 clip popularized by economist and The Argument contributor Phil Magness, then-Sen. Vance presented a take he called “maybe super heterodox”:

“I am not sure that I think the reserve currency is actually good for the United States of America. I think there is a good argument that reserve currency status is akin to coal in Appalachia — it’s a resource curse, right? It allows your consumers to consume very cheaply. Right? That’s been the story of the American economy for the last 15 or so years, even before that, is we can just borrow, basically in an unlimited way, because we have the reserve currency.”

Personally, I think the benefits of the dollar as reserve currency can be slightly overblown — as former Federal Reserve Chair Ben Bernanke explained in 2016, other countries, like Canada, Germany, and the United Kingdom, were able to borrow more cheaply than we were.

But the actual debate over reserve currencies is, to me, beside the point. What’s more interesting is Vance’s strange distaste for “consumers.”

The U.S. dollar’s status as the world’s reserve currency creates a huge demand for dollars, which makes our currency stronger relative to other nations’. That means it takes fewer dollars to buy things priced in Chinese yuan or Japanese yen than it otherwise would.

If a Japanese car costs 1 million yen and $1 = 100 yen, then the car costs $10,000. But if $1 = 150 yen, then the car costs about $6,700.

Vance thinks that this is bad. He would like you to pay $10,000 for a Japanese car. Why? Because he thinks it would make you buy American and because he thinks it would make foreigners buy American (because our currency would be weaker).

As the straight logic goes, Vance is right: If you made it more expensive to buy Hondas, more people would buy GM. But does that mean more people would be better off?

Subscribe now

At the peak of manufacturing in 1979, 19.6 million Americans worked in the sector. No one really thinks we’re getting back to this, because modern factories are much more automated. Even boosters of the Vance agenda like the Conservative Partnership Institute’s Rachel Bovard have pivoted to talking about increasing manufacturing output rather than jobs.

But let’s say for the sake of argument that we were going to return to 1979 levels. Let’s even scale that to today’s population, which would mean roughly 30 million working in manufacturing.

That’s just 8.7% of the country. So, in order to pull people out of whatever they’re doing to instead manufacture cars or clothes or plastics, Vance seeks to make almost 350 million Americans (including those now working in manufacturing) pay thousands of dollars more for critical goods like computers, phones, and vehicles.

What’s bizarre about all of this is that there are entire strains of industrial policy that aren’t hostile to the American consumer. A normal, recurring view within economic debates is that markets underinvest in certain capabilities — like basic science, infrastructure, workforce training, and supply-chain redundancies — so the government should step in and build or subsidize those capacities.

Vance’s worldview differentiates itself through its hostility to the idea of low prices for consumer goods. He is part of a long line of “producerists“ who believe that the economy’s moral purpose is to reward producers rather than maximize consumer well-being.

Who does this leave out? The roughly 50% of Americans who are not in the workforce: children, retirees, disabled people, students, and stay-at-home parents.

But at its core, I just don’t think being a consumer is somehow embarrassing. To be alive is to consume. I consume clean air and water, clothing, books, pens, glasses, medical care, legal services, train tickets, and so many more things.

These are not signs of decadence; they’re signs of human flourishing.

If you are lucky, for most of your life, you will not be working. But regardless of how things are going, you will be consuming. Every producer is also a consumer, and every consumer makes a producer’s work possible.2

That’s why it’s good for the government to prioritize consumer well-being — and why a producerist politics necessarily devalues people and stages of life that are less “productive.”
